blocks.content: 1. WHAT IS MATTER?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Matter is defined as anything that possesses mass and occupies space.
The physical states of matter (solid, liquid, gas) can be interchanged by altering temperature and pressure.
Evaporation is a surface phenomenon occurring at any temperature below a liquid's boiling point.
Evaporation results in cooling because particles absorb heat energy from the surroundings to compensate for energy lost during vaporization.
Sublimation is the direct conversion of a solid to a gaseous state without entering the intermediate liquid state.
Latent heat of fusion is the heat required to convert a solid into a liquid at its melting point without raising its temperature.

blocks.content:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.

This means:

• If something has weight → it is matter

• If something occupies space → it is matter



Everything we see around us is made of matter.

For example:

• Air

• Water

• Food

• Book

• Chair

• Human body



Even air is matter because it occupies space and has mass.
2. CHARACTERISTICS OF MATTER

Matter has some basic characteristics which help us to understand its nature.



1. Matter has mass:

This means matter has weight.

For example, a book is heavier than a paper.



2. Matter occupies space:

Anything that occupies space is matter.

For example, air fills a balloon.



3. Matter is made of very tiny particles:

These particles are so small that we cannot see them with naked eyes.



4. Particles of matter have space between them:

That is why substances can be compressed.



5. Particles of matter are in continuous motion:

This motion increases when temperature increases.



6. Particles of matter attract each other:

This force of attraction is strongest in solids and weakest in gases.
3. STATES OF MATTER

Matter exists in three main physical states:

1. Solid

2. Liquid

3. Gas



These states differ due to difference in:

• Intermolecular force

• Space between particles

• Movement of particles
3.1 SOLID STATE

Solids have fixed shape and fixed volume.



In solids:

• Particles are very close to each other

• Force of attraction is very strong

• Particles only vibrate at their place

• Solids are rigid

• Solids cannot be compressed



Examples:

• Stone

• Iron

• Wood

• Brick
3.2 LIQUID STATE

Liquids have fixed volume but no fixed shape.



In liquids:

• Particles are less tightly packed than solids

• Force of attraction is weaker than solids

• Particles can move freely

• Liquids can flow

• Liquids take the shape of container



Examples:

• Water

• Milk

• Oil
3.3 GASEOUS STATE

Gases have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.

In gases:

• Particles are very far apart

• Force of attraction is very weak

• Particles move freely in all directions

• Gases are highly compressible



Examples:

• Oxygen

• Nitrogen

• Carbon dioxide
4. CHANGE OF STATE OF MATTER
EVAPORATION (VERY IMPORTANT)

Matter can change its state by changing:

• Temperature

• Pressure



When heat is supplied or removed, particles gain or lose energy and change their state.
4.1 MELTING

Melting is the process in which a solid changes into liquid on heating.



Example:

Ice → Water



The temperature at which a solid melts is called its melting point.



Melting point of ice = 0°C



At melting point:

• Temperature remains constant

• Heat is used to break intermolecular forces
4.2 FREEZING

Freezing is the process in which a liquid changes into solid on cooling.



Example:

Water → Ice



Freezing point of water = 0°C

4.3 BOILING

Boiling is the process in which a liquid changes into gas at a fixed temperature.

Boiling point of water = 100°C



At boiling point:

• Vapour pressure becomes equal to atmospheric pressure

• Temperature remains constant
4.4 EVAPORATION (VERY IMPORTANT)

Evaporation is the slow change of liquid into vapour at any temperature.



Evaporation occurs only at the surface of the liquid.



Examples:

• Drying of clothes

• Cooling of water in earthen pot

• Sweating cools our body

rows: Occurs at any temperature below boiling point
Occurs only at a specific fixed boiling point

blocks.content: Why Evaporation Causes Cooling?

During evaporation, high energy particles escape first.

Remaining particles lose energy.

This lowers the temperature of the liquid.

Hence, evaporation causes cooling.
Factors Affecting Evaporation

1. Surface Area – Larger area → Faster evaporation

2. Temperature – Higher temperature → Faster evaporation

3. Wind Speed – Higher wind speed → Faster evaporation

4. Humidity – Lower humidity → Faster evaporation
4.5 SUBLIMATION

Sublimation is the direct change of solid into gas without passing through liquid state.



Examples:

• Camphor

• Naphthalene

• Ammonium chloride
5. LATENT HEAT (VERY IMPORTANT)

Latent heat is the heat required to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature.



During change of state:

• Heat is absorbed or released

• Temperature remains constant
5.1 LATENT HEAT OF FUSION

items: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon, whereas boiling is a bulk phenomenon.
Latent heat does not raise the temperature of the substance during a change of state.
Solid Carbon Dioxide (Dry Ice) directly converts to gas when pressure is reduced to 1 atmosphere.
Rate of evaporation increases with an increase in surface area, temperature, and wind speed, but decreases with higher humidity.

blocks.content:
It is the amount of heat required to change 1 kg of solid into liquid at its melting point.

Example:

Ice → Water

Temperature remains 0°C during the process.
5.2 LATENT HEAT OF VAPORIZATION

It is the amount of heat required to convert 1 kg of liquid into gas at its boiling point.

Steam has more energy than boiling water.
6. EFFECT OF PRESSURE

Increasing pressure reduces space between particles.

Due to high pressure:

• Gas can be converted into liquid

Example:

LPG is stored in cylinder by applying high pressure.
7. FINAL REVISION POINTS

• Matter has mass and occupies space

• Three states of matter

• Change of state occurs due to heat

• Evaporation causes cooling

• Latent heat changes state, not temperature

• Steam has more energy than water
